title: Ethiopia Retakes Adigrat as Its War With Eritrea Escalates, Sudan Buries 72 Miners Killed on the Egyptian Border, and Pakistan Jails Hundreds Under Emergency Rule
subhead: While attention stays fixed on Riyadh and the Gulf, two interstate wars and a democracy crackdown in South Asia moved sharply forward — a Horn of Africa conflict drawing in drones and foreign patrons, a strike on Sudanese gold miners that kills 72, and Pakistan's army-backed suspension of an entire provincial government.

sections.heading: Ethiopia and Eritrea Slide Toward Open War
sections.body:
Ethiopian forces regained control of the Tigrayan city of Adigrat after Eritrean troops withdrew, according to the Oman Observer and Al Jazeera, which reported celebrations in the city. The recapture follows a reported Eritrean incursion into Ethiopia's Tigray and, allegedly, Afar regions that escalated through late September and early October.

The two countries were allies as recently as the 2020-2022 Tigray war, when Eritrean forces fought alongside Ethiopia's military against the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF). That partnership has collapsed. Addis Ababa this month accused Asmara of financing the TPLF insurgency, closed its embassy in Eritrea, and ordered ten Eritrean diplomats out; Eritrea's foreign ministry responded by severing all diplomatic ties and told an Egyptian diplomat to leave within 48 hours. According to the Reuters-cited monitoring group ACLED, drones have been targeting Eritrean troops inside Ethiopia, suggesting both external supply chains and a widening battlefield. The Eritrean deployment has been estimated at roughly 6,000 troops.

Eritrea's intervention matters far beyond the Horn. It reactivates a front that the 2022 Pretoria agreement was supposed to freeze, threatens the Red Sea's western shore at a moment when shipping through Bab al-Mandab is already under Houthi pressure, and risks pulling in Egypt — which is already locked in a Nile-dam dispute with Ethiopia.
sections.whyItMatters: A second interstate war on the Red Sea's western flank compounds the shipping crisis already driven by the Houthis. A hostile Ethiopia-Eritrea border also removes a stabilising buffer around Tigray and invites Egyptian involvement.

sections.heading: Sudan: 72 Killed in Airstrike on Gold Miners at the Egyptian Border
sections.body:
An airstrike struck an artisanal gold-mining site in a mountainous area along the Sudan-Egypt border, killing at least 72 people, according to Sky News. The attack is the deadliest single incident reported in Sudan in recent weeks and adds to a documented pattern of war crimes in the conflict.

It came as the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) continued attacks across multiple states. On October 9, an RSF drone strike on a displaced-persons site in Blue Nile State killed 41, per AP. Days later, a drone strike hit a dormitory at the University of Kordofan in El Obeid, North Kordofan, killing five, according to the Sudan Tribune.

The border location is significant: Egypt has quietly backed Sudan's armed forces against the RSF, and strikes near the frontier raise the prospect of spillover into Egyptian territory. Sudan's gold trade, much of it artisanal and smuggled, is a key revenue source for the warring parties, making mining sites both economic targets and sites of atrocity.
sections.whyItMatters: Sudan's war is now the world's largest displacement and hunger crisis, and attacks are creeping toward Egypt's border. The gold trade funding both sides is also a channel for external patrons, including Gulf states.

sections.heading: Pakistan Suspends an Entire Provincial Government and Jails Hundreds
sections.body:
Pakistan's federal government suspended the PTI-led administration in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, imposed emergency rule, and detained hundreds of Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf members, including former provincial chief minister Sohail Afridi, according to AFP via RFI. The crackdown followed the imposition of a state of emergency in the province, which borders Afghanistan.

The move effectively decapitates Imran Khan's party in its single remaining provincial stronghold and coincides with a separate escalation along the Afghan frontier: Pakistan launched airstrikes inside Afghanistan, claiming it killed 22 Taliban fighters, while Kabul said nine women and children died in Kunar and Helmand provinces, per Al Jazeera.

Stacking a domestic political crackdown on a live cross-border war is a notable escalation. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has been the epicenter of Pakistan's long-running fight with the TTP, and removing elected provincial leadership during active hostilities with Afghanistan concentrates both military and political authority in the center.
sections.whyItMatters: Nuclear-armed Pakistan is simultaneously fighting inside Afghanistan and suppressing its main opposition party — a combination that raises risks on both its western border and its internal stability, with Saudi Arabia and China both closely invested in Islamabad's cohesion.

sections.heading: Riyadh's Airport Stays Shut as Houthi Strikes Continue and Washington Weighs In
sections.body:
The Houthis claimed a third consecutive day of ballistic-missile attacks on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on October 12, according to Reuters. Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority extended the suspension of operations at the airport, telling airlines flights would halt until at least October 15 to verify safety, AFP reported via The Hindu. Riyadh Metro suspended service to three stations serving the airport.

The campaign, spanning October 6-12, has killed at least 20 people and injured more than 370 across attacks on airports in Riyadh, Abha, and Dammam, per Wikipedia's tally of cited reports — the deadliest series of attacks in Saudi Arabia since 2015. A 13-year-old toll figure rose when an Indian national injured on October 10 died of his wounds, Reuters reported. The Wall Street Journal reported that the October 10 strike on Terminal 3 alone killed 12 and injured 309.

The strategic core of the story is the question of US involvement. Sky News reported that President Trump said the United States would 'look at' joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis. That would be a qualitative change: direct US participation in the Yemen war would merge the Gulf and Yemen theaters and reverse Washington's posture of keeping the Yemen file separate from the Iran conflict.
sections.whyItMatters: Saudi Arabia's flagship airport has been shut for days by a non-state actor, a severe hit to Gulf prestige and aviation. If Washington joins the strikes, the Yemen war fuses with the broader Iran conflict and multiplies US exposure.

sections.heading: Hormuz: Tanker Hit by Projectile, Drone Strike Off Oman's Coast
sections.body:
The UK Maritime Trade Operations reported that a tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz was hit by an unknown projectile, according to Middle East Eye. Separately, a drone struck the Nicaragua-flagged tanker MT Petro Dolphin near Sohar, Oman, leaving two Indian sailors missing and prompting the rescue of nine others, AFP reported via Arab News. Omani authorities launched search-and-rescue operations.

The Petro Dolphin attack is notable because it occurred near Oman, the very mediator that has been brokering Hormuz de-escalation. Striking a vessel in Omani waters undercuts Muscat's ability to guarantee safe passage — the premise of the talks that have repeatedly failed to produce a durable arrangement.

The Strait remains the single most consequential choke point in the global energy system, and the combination of sustained tanker attacks and renewed Houthi missile strikes on Gulf infrastructure keeps shipping and insurance costs elevated independent of any diplomatic headline.
sections.whyItMatters: Attacks are now hitting the waters of the mediator state itself, eroding the mechanism that has kept Hormuz partially open. Continued disruption keeps energy and freight prices high and narrows the space for any negotiated reopening.

sections.heading: Quick Hits: US Politics, Ukraine, and the Nobel Economics Prize
sections.body: Trump said the US military will not attack Iran before next month's midterm elections, per AP — effectively putting the Iran war on a political clock. The USS Abraham Lincoln returned to San Diego after a nearly seven-month deployment, per The Guardian and Los Angeles Times, a partial drawdown at a moment of continued Gulf tension. In Ukraine, a Russian airstrike on a five-story residential building in Zaporizhzhia killed at least 20 and injured 18, according to Ukrainska Pravda. And American economists Robert Ernest Hall and Michael Dean Woodford won the 2026 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for work on the microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation, CNN reported.
sections.whyItMatters: The pre-election pause in US action against Iran may be temporary, but it freezes decision-making in the Gulf for a month. Meanwhile the Ukraine war continues with mass-casualty strikes on civilian housing, showing the energy-ceasefire talk has not translated into reduced violence on the ground.

bottomLine: Today's most consequential news was not in the headlines most feeds led with: Ethiopia's recapture of Adigrat marks an escalating interstate war with Eritrea on the Red Sea's western shore, Sudan's war reached Egypt's border with a strike that killed 72 gold miners, and Pakistan jailed hundreds of opposition figures while fighting inside Afghanistan. These are the kind of developments that reshape regional order while the Gulf dominates coverage. Meanwhile, in that Gulf, Riyadh's airport remains shut after a third day of Houthi missile strikes, the US president is openly weighing joining the war in Yemen, and attacks have now reached the waters of Oman — the mediator that has kept Hormuz partly open. Watch whether Washington crosses the line into the Yemen war: that, more than any single strike, would determine whether the region's separate conflicts merge into one.
